headline: The first Christian to be killed died asking for his killers to be forgiven.
body: Stephen was stoned outside Jerusalem after a speech that surveyed the whole history of Israel. Luke records that he prayed for those throwing the stones, and that the coats were laid at the feet of a young man named Saul, who approved of the killing.

headline: They called him camel-knees.
body: James, who led the church in Jerusalem, was remembered by the nickname his congregation gave him: his knees had grown callused as a camel's from the time he spent kneeling in the temple. He was thrown from the parapet and clubbed to death around 62.

headline: They left the city before the siege, and were criticised for it for centuries.
body: Eusebius reports that the Jerusalem church, warned by an oracle, withdrew across the Jordan to Pella before Rome destroyed the city in 70. The departure preserved the community and permanently strained its relations with those who stayed.

headline: The slave girl outlasted everyone.
body: In the persecution at Lyons in 177, Blandina was a young slave whom her companions feared would break first. She was tortured from morning until evening and outlasted her torturers, who gave up exhausted; she was killed last, after watching the others die.

headline: During the plague they went toward the sick rather than away.
body: Dionysius of Alexandria described Christians nursing the infected and taking the disease themselves, while others abandoned the dying in the streets and fled. Historians have argued since that this behaviour, more than any argument, explains much of the church's growth.

headline: She followed her son across the Mediterranean and would not stop praying.
body: Monica prayed for Augustine's conversion for over thirty years, followed him from Africa to Italy when he slipped away from her, and was told by a bishop that the son of such tears could not be lost. She died shortly after he was baptised.

headline: A bishop barred an emperor from communion until he repented.
body: After Theodosius ordered a massacre at Thessalonica, Ambrose of Milan refused him the sacrament and required public penance. The emperor submitted. It set a precedent, argued over ever since, that civil power is not beyond the church's discipline.

headline: No council invented the canon; they ratified what was already being read.
body: By the time North African councils listed the books of Scripture at the end of the fourth century, the churches had been reading substantially that collection for generations. The lists settled disputed edges rather than deciding the centre.

headline: He lived on top of a pillar for thirty-seven years and became a counsellor to emperors.
body: Simeon the Stylite withdrew to a platform on a column near Aleppo to escape the crowds that came to see him. The crowds came anyway. He preached from the top twice a day, arbitrated disputes, and corresponded with emperors.

headline: He sailed until he could no longer see Ireland, and stopped there.
body: Columba left Ireland after a dispute that turned bloody, reportedly resolving to win as many souls as had died. He settled on Iona, a small island off the Scottish coast, and the monastery there evangelised much of Scotland and northern England.

headline: Kings and bishops came to a woman for advice, and five of her monks became bishops.
body: Hilda ruled the double monastery at Whitby, housing both men and women, and hosted the synod that decided the English church's direction. Bede records that so great was her prudence that not only ordinary people but kings and princes sought her counsel.

headline: He finished dictating the last sentence of John's gospel and then died.
body: Bede spent his final days translating John into English. His pupil recorded the scene: told there was one sentence left, Bede said write it quickly, dictated it, asked to be turned toward the place where he prayed, and died.

headline: A king who thought learning had collapsed set about translating books himself.
body: Alfred of Wessex found that hardly anyone south of the Humber could read the services they recited. He organised translations of the books he judged most necessary, and by his own account worked on some of them personally, between wars.

headline: The reform worked because the founder gave up control of it.
body: When Cluny was founded in 910 its patron placed it directly under the pope rather than under local lords or bishops, insulating it from the politics that had corrupted other houses. From that independence came two centuries of monastic reform across Europe.

headline: Mothers were said to hide their sons when he came to town.
body: Bernard of Clairvaux was so effective a recruiter for the Cistercians that families reportedly kept young men out of his way. He also advised popes, arbitrated between kingdoms, and wrote some of the tenderest devotional prose of the Middle Ages.

headline: A merchant gave his money away and started preaching. It was the preaching that got him condemned.
body: Peter Waldo of Lyons had the Gospels translated into the vernacular and began preaching as a layman. The poverty was tolerated; unlicensed preaching was not. His followers were driven into the Alpine valleys and survived there for centuries.

headline: The first clause of Magna Carta is about the church.
body: Before any of the famous provisions about justice and taxation, the charter opens by granting that the English church shall be free. Archbishop Stephen Langton was central to the negotiations, and the document has ecclesiastical fingerprints throughout.

headline: Parish priests died at a higher rate than their parishioners.
body: Because their work took them to the bedsides of the dying to hear confessions, clergy mortality in the Black Death ran above the general rate in many places. Whole parishes were left without ministers, and the hasty replacements that followed became a standing grievance.

headline: He printed the Greek New Testament and lit a fuse he then tried to stamp out.
body: Erasmus published the Greek text in 1516 with his own Latin translation alongside, exposing places where the Vulgate had gone astray. Reformers seized on it. Erasmus spent the rest of his life arguing publicly with Luther and refusing to leave the Roman church.

headline: The Swiss Reformation began, more or less, with a sausage.
body: In Lent 1522 a printer in Zurich served sausages to a gathering that included Zwingli, who did not eat but defended those who did — arguing that Scripture nowhere commanded the fast. The ensuing dispute pushed the city into reform.

headline: They were drowned for baptising adults, in a grim joke about their convictions.
body: The first adult baptisms among the Swiss Brethren in 1525 broke with both Rome and Zurich's reformers. Authorities on all sides persecuted them, and execution by drowning was used pointedly. Their descendants include the Mennonites, Hutterites and Amish.

headline: He put the doctrine into songs because people remember songs.
body: Luther held that music was next to theology, and wrote hymns in German for congregations that had listened silently for generations. A Mighty Fortress is his; so is the practice, now unremarkable, of everyone in the building singing.

headline: She escaped a convent in a fish barrel and then ran the household economy.
body: Katharina von Bora fled her convent with eleven others, hidden in a merchant's wagon among herring barrels. She married Luther, and managed the brewery, farm, garden and boarding house that supported a home permanently full of students and guests.

headline: She reformed her order while under investigation by the Inquisition.
body: Teresa of Avila founded reformed Carmelite houses across Spain, travelling constantly in poor health, while her writings on prayer were being examined for error. She was made a Doctor of the Church four hundred years later.

headline: He found the same presence among the pots and pans as at the altar.
body: A lay brother who spent decades in a Paris monastery kitchen, which he disliked, Nicholas Herman said he had learned to possess God in as great tranquillity there as on his knees. The conversations recorded by a visitor became The Practice of the Presence of God.

headline: They found the note sewn into his coat after he died.
body: Pascal recorded an intense experience one November night on a scrap of parchment — beginning with the word FIRE, and distinguishing the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob from the God of the philosophers. He carried it stitched inside his clothing for the rest of his life.

headline: They argued for days over single words, and the minutes survive.
body: The Westminster divines debated wording with a thoroughness that reads as excruciating — sessions spent on a phrase, votes retaken, committees appointed to reword committees. The care is why the documents have held together for four centuries.

headline: He catechised his whole parish family by family, and it changed the town.
body: Richard Baxter worked through Kidderminster household by household, spending an hour with each. He reckoned it did more good than his preaching. He wrote The Reformed Pastor to argue that other ministers should do the same.

headline: Two thousand ministers gave up their livings on a single day.
body: The Act of Uniformity required assent to everything in the Prayer Book by St Bartholomew's Day 1662. Around two thousand clergy refused and were ejected, losing income and homes. English Nonconformity dates from that day.

headline: They would not remove their hats for anyone, and were jailed for it.
body: George Fox and the early Quakers refused hat-honour and swore no oaths, on the ground that all people stand equal before God. It read as sedition. Thousands were imprisoned, and their refusal to swear kept them out of public life for generations.

headline: The most famous preacher in the colonies was voted out by his own congregation.
body: Jonathan Edwards was dismissed from Northampton in 1750 after a dispute over who could receive communion. He went to a frontier mission at Stockbridge, and there wrote the philosophical works his reputation now rests on.

headline: He thought open-air preaching was almost sinful, and then did it for fifty years.
body: Wesley recorded that he could scarcely reconcile himself to preaching in the fields, having been so tenacious of decency and order that he had thought saving souls outside a church almost a sin. Whitefield talked him into it, and he never stopped.

headline: He crossed the Appalachians sixty times on horseback.
body: Francis Asbury organised Methodism across the American frontier by riding it, covering something like 270,000 miles in forty-five years and ordaining preachers who did the same. The circuit rider reached settlements no settled ministry could.

headline: Sunday school began as a literacy programme for children who worked six days a week.
body: Robert Raikes started classes in Gloucester in 1780 for children employed in the pin factories, teaching reading on the one day they were free — using the Bible because it was the book available. Within decades hundreds of thousands were enrolled.

headline: He spent a career on unglamorous bills about hours and chimneys.
body: Lord Shaftesbury pushed through legislation on factory hours, child labour in mines, the treatment of the mentally ill, and the use of small boys as chimney sweeps. He described the work as tedious and said he could not stop while the abuses continued.

headline: He housed thousands of orphans and refused ever to ask anyone for money.
body: George Muller ran orphanages in Bristol on the stated principle of asking God only, publishing detailed accounts each year partly as evidence. Over sixty years he cared for more than ten thousand children, and the books balanced.

headline: She recorded the date she believed God called her, and then waited sixteen years.
body: Florence Nightingale wrote down a call received in February 1837 and spent years fighting her family for permission to train. What she eventually did with statistics and sanitation in military hospitals reduced mortality and founded modern nursing.

headline: She wrote home demanding that women be sent as missionaries, not just wives.
body: Lottie Moon worked in Shandong for nearly forty years and pressed her board relentlessly to fund and appoint single women. During a famine she shared her own rations to the point of starvation and died on the voyage home, weighing fifty pounds.

headline: He wrote it knowing he was dying, and preached his last sermon the same day.
body: Henry Francis Lyte was consumptive and leaving his Devon parish for the last time when he wrote Abide With Me. He died within months. The hymn is sung at funerals, at coronations, and every year before the FA Cup Final.

headline: He wrote it crossing the water where his four daughters had drowned.
body: Horatio Spafford's four daughters died when their ship sank in the Atlantic; his wife's telegram read: saved alone. Travelling out to meet her, he passed near the place it happened, and wrote the hymn that begins When peace like a river attendeth my way.
